text: The goal of demand flexibility is to change the electric or gas load profile of the building in a meaningful way; therefore, this measure is applicable to all dwelling units with either a cooling system or a heating system. Although the measure shifts the load profile of the dwelling units with nonelectric heating during heating season, the change to the electric load profile is minimal because it only changes the fan or pump electricity consumption. For this reason, the heating load analysis in this document is focused on buildings with electric heating only. This measure modifies the existing building energy model thermostat set point schedules during the pre-peak and on-peak periods only. For times outside of the event, the existing thermostat schedules in the model are unchanged. If the baseline thermostat set point schedules indicate that the dwelling unit is already in a setback or a setup state, the demand flexibility thermostat change still applies. The load flexibility scenario (which includes the pre-peak duration and the set point offset values) serves as input for the measure, allowing customized controls. The input values used for this measure are explained in section 3.3 Input Variables. Figure 2. Modeling approach for running a load flexibility measure in ResStock Values for on-peak hours for summer months, winter months, and intermediate months are provided at the state level in an input file. The load flexibility measure first retrieves the heating and cooling set point schedules specific to each individual dwelling unit. It then modifies these schedules by adjusting the set points by an offset during the designated pre-peak and on-peak periods. This approach ensures that each unit’s load flexibility aligns with its original comfort settings while providing targeted adjustments to reduce energy
